1.pericope_label: Absalom’s chariot and runners, his court at the city gate, and the stealing of Israel’s hearts

schools.summary: Henry sharpens the display into a charge: the son had learned of the king of Geshur to multiply horses, a thing forbidden to the kings of Israel, so that he looked desirable while his father on a mule looked despicable, and the people who had wanted a king like the nations now had one. At the gate he has him out before the king’s other sons were stirring, prying into every man’s city so as to inform himself of the whole kingdom, and embracing whoever offered obeisance while his heart was as proud as Lucifer’s — ambitious projects being often carried on under a show of humility, and fawning on the people in order to betray them being abominable hypocrisy. On the complaint that no man was deputed to hear causes he observes that it is the way of turbulent and aspiring men to reproach the government they are under, and that even David could not escape the worst of censures. His hardest sentence falls on the wish to be judge: a man who should himself have been judged to death for murder had the impudence to aim at judging others, and those are commonly most ambitious of preferment who are least fit for it; he wanted no subordinate place, though under his own father, but must be supreme or nothing, never considering what a fatigue it would be to have every man come to him, since Moses himself could not bear it. He adds that a bad cause can always be given a good colour when its owner tells the story.
Gill reads the early rising as a demonstration of how industrious the man would be in office, and notes that the cause was approved on the hearing of one side only.

Ellicott treats the splendour as a necessary preparation for revolt, as it was afterwards for Adonijah, and notes that this is the first use in Israel of chariots and horses as regal state. He explains the office behind the complaint — the king could not hear every case, so appointed men heard causes and reported the facts — and then names the art: the claimant does not accuse the king of wrong but insinuates that the system is defective and professes his own wish to set it right, which is what the demagogue has done in every age. Keil and Delitzsch add a classical parallel, that Agamemnon is said to have secured the command of the Grecian army by conduct of just this kind, and insist that the closing phrase means not to deceive but to steal the heart, that is, to bring a man over secretly and by stratagem.

Clarke reproduces Calmet’s character of the man — bold, revengeful, haughty, magnificent, eloquent and popular — who after his brother’s death saw no hindrance to the throne, being royal by both parents, and whose sin was simply that he sought it in his father’s lifetime; he adds that the man was versed in those arts, that the common people heard him gladly, and that like all pretended patriots he found fault with men in power only because he wanted their places, meaning to act as they did or worse. Wesley has him act as eldest surviving son, Amnon being dead and Chileab dead or incapable, with the display calculated to make the people conclude the succession already settled on him; at the gate he reads a show of solicitude for the public and for every private person, forestalling each man with an offer of help, and he supplies the slanders behind the complaint — the other sons and the judges corrupt or careless, the father too old to mind public affairs.

debates.question: What was Absalom doing by rising early and standing beside the way of the gate?

positions.view: Showing how industrious he would be in office
Making a show of solicitude for the public and for every private person
Prying into every man’s city so as to inform himself of the whole kingdom

outliers.claim: Alone in bringing a classical parallel, that Agamemnon secured the command of the Grecian army by conduct of just this kind.
Alone in noting that this is the first appearance in Israel of chariots and horses as regal state.

themes: fifty runners before the chariot
a court kept at the gate
no man deputed of the king to hear thee
ambition under a show of humility
stealing the heart by stratagem

7.pericope_label: The vow at Hebron, the trumpet-borne proclamation, and Ahithophel’s defection to the conspiracy

schools.summary: Henry keeps the forty years and moves the starting point, dating them from the change of the government into a monarchy some ten years before David’s accession, which puts the revolt in the king’s thirtieth year. He suspects no vow was ever made, since a man who stuck at neither murder nor treason would not make conscience of a lie and nobody could disprove him. Hebron he makes a royal city in the heart of Judah where the son’s interest was strong and his father’s reign had begun, and he explains why men known to be loyal were worth inviting: the common people would conclude they had gone over, and the king was deserted by his best friends. He then remarks, in nearly the words Wesley uses, that it is no new thing for good men and good things to be used by designing men to colour bad practices.

Gill canvasses six reckonings of the forty years — from Israel’s first king, from the slaying of the priests at Nob, from the anointing by Samuel and others — finds none of them satisfactory, and is tempted to conclude that the copy has forty for four. He reports a Jewish tradition about the two hundred guests, that leave was given to invite only two, and that the host asked two more unknown to the first, and so on two by two to two hundred. On the counsellor’s desertion he thinks the man may have been Bathsheba’s grandfather, resenting the adultery and the death of Uriah.

Ellicott calls the figure certainly incorrect, since the son was born after his father began to reign and that reign was only forty years, and prefers the four of the Syriac, most Vulgate manuscripts and Josephus. He alone allows that the vow may have been genuinely made in exile, however plainly it is now used as a pretext, and he adds to the choice of Hebron that many there may have resented the removal of the court to Jerusalem. He takes the two hundred for prominent citizens whose ignorance shows how close the secret was kept, and whom their host meant either to win at Hebron or to prevent from opposing him. On the counsellor he sets out the Bathsheba conjecture and dismisses it, the names in the two genealogies not being demonstrably one man, and a grandfather being likelier to have felt honoured than aggrieved that his granddaughter was made queen; he proposes instead that this counsellor and many others of Judah were alienated as their relative importance shrank in a growing empire, and notes that the revolt was cradled in Judah. Keil and Delitzsch agree that the number is altogether unsuitable, fitting neither the son’s age nor any year of the reign, and reject the expedient, used by several of the Rabbins, of counting from Saul’s accession; they share the Hebron resentment, and stress with Ellicott that the agents were to sound the people first and declare themselves only where they found support.

Clarke notes that no Hebrew manuscript yet discovered supports four, and prefers another correction, two of Kennicott’s manuscripts reading forty days, which he thinks likelier than the received text; he remarks on the pose of a strict worshipper maintained even in a heathen country, makes the trumpet a kind of telegraph, trumpet exciting trumpet from place to place until in a few minutes all Israel had the proclamation, and observes that in gaining this counsellor the rebel gained the prime minister. Wesley also keeps the forty and dates them from the monarchy, has the sacrifices offered in no devotion to God but as a pretence for calling great numbers together, agrees on Hebron, and makes with Henry the same remark about good men and good things used to colour bad practices.

debates.question: How are the forty years of verse 7 to be read?

positions.view: Certainly incorrect; read four, with the Syriac, most Vulgate manuscripts and Josephus
Altogether unsuitable, and not to be rescued by counting from Saul’s accession
Six reckonings tried and none satisfactory; probably the copy has forty for four
Forty days, from two of Kennicott’s manuscripts, no Hebrew manuscript supporting four
Forty kept, dated from the change of the government into a monarchy

debates.question: Was the vow Absalom pleaded a real one?

positions.view: No vow was ever made; the man would not make conscience of a lie
The sacrifices were a pretence for calling great numbers together, with no devotion to God
It may have been genuinely made in exile, however plainly it is now used as a pretext

debates.question: Why did Ahithophel desert to Absalom?

positions.view: A private grievance; he may have been Bathsheba’s grandfather, resenting the adultery and Uriah’s death
That conjecture fails; he and many of Judah were alienated as their importance shrank in a growing empire

outliers.claim: Alone in preferring the reading forty days from two of Kennicott’s manuscripts, and alone in describing the trumpet as a kind of telegraph.
Alone in reporting the tradition that the two hundred were invited two by two, each pair unknown to the last.

themes: a vow remembered out of Geshur
trumpet exciting trumpet
two hundred guests who knew nothing
the prime minister gone over
a revolt cradled in Judah

13.pericope_label: The flight from Jerusalem, the six hundred out of Gath, and Ittai’s refusal to turn back

schools.summary: Gill notices only that the news came to the king by a messenger, perhaps one of the two hundred who got away when the design appeared.

Keil and Delitzsch suspect the king feared betrayal, and read the flight as a measure to prevent a massacre and to give his adherents time to gather; they take the halting-place for a proper name, the far house, the last on the outskirts before the road crossed the Kidron. On the six hundred they call the name strange, since actual Philistines cannot be meant, and hold the apposition to identify them as the old companions in arms who gathered to David in his flight from Saul; they add that Ittai brought his whole family, and reject Thenius’s view that he came as a hostage as founded on a misreading. The grace and truth of the parting blessing they refer to God’s own. Ellicott judges the king’s course vindicated by the sequel, since both of the rebel’s own counsellors saw that delay would be fatal to an unreasonable cause; he agrees on the far house, argues the six hundred to be the body traceable through Keilah, the wilderness, Gath, Ziklag and Hebron and supposes them the later mighty men, and denies that the king either recognises his son as king or speaks ironically — reading the clause as a stranger and an exile at thy place, he has the king tell a foreigner that the quarrel is no concern of his and that he may serve whoever holds power in fact. He sets the reply beside Ruth’s.

Clarke alone accounts for so general a defection, offering seven reasons: that the king was old and could not attend to justice; that no judges were properly appointed; that Joab’s power had grown oppressive and the king dared not execute the law against him; that partisans of Saul’s house still thought the crown unfairly got; that the king lay under God’s displeasure for Bathsheba and Uriah; that every state has men who can never rest; and that the son was the undisputed heir, most people being readier to hail the rising than the setting sun. He says this was the first time David turned his back on an enemy and finds no military reason for it, the city being so strong that the blind and the lame had once been thought defence enough, and the guard and the six hundred still his; he reads the departure instead as submission, the king taking all as from the hand of God, weeping, going barefoot, covering his head and not even hastening, since the habit of mourners is not that of men fleeing before enemies. He reports that the six hundred are generally supposed proselytes and that some take their leader for a son of the king of Gath, banished for attachment to David. Wesley gives a military reason instead: Zion was strong but unprovisioned, and once shut in the king would have lost the kingdom, where by marching out he could raise an army. He reads the six hundred the other way, as Philistines by birth of the city or territory of Gath, won by David’s counsel and example to the true religion, which is why their leader is called a stranger and they his brethren; he takes the instruction to abide with the king of the usurper, now made king, with whom a man whose settled home is in Jerusalem may properly remain, and the parting blessing for a prayer that God would make good to a true-hearted proselyte the promises given not to Israelites only.

debates.question: Why did David leave Jerusalem instead of standing a siege?

positions.view: Not for any military reason, but in submission, taking all as from the hand of God
Because Zion was strong but unprovisioned; marching out he could raise an army
Because he feared betrayal, and would prevent a massacre and gain his adherents time
The course is vindicated by the sequel, delay being fatal to the rebel’s unreasonable cause

debates.question: Who were the six hundred men that came after the king out of Gath?

positions.view: Old Hebrew companions in arms, gathered to David in his flight from Saul; actual Philistines cannot be meant
Philistines by birth, of Gath, won to the true religion, hence a stranger and his brethren
Generally supposed proselytes, their leader perhaps a banished son of the king of Gath

debates.question: Which king is Ittai told to return and abide with?

positions.view: The usurper, now made king, with whom a settled citizen of Jerusalem may properly remain
Whoever holds power in fact; neither a recognition of Absalom nor an irony

outliers.claim: Alone in setting out a list of seven reasons for the general defection, and alone in observing that this was the first time David turned his back on an enemy.
Alone in setting Ittai’s reply beside Ruth’s.

themes: the far house on the outskirts
barefoot and with covered head
six hundred who came out of Gath
whither thou goest thither will thy servant be
the brook Kidron crossed

24.pericope_label: The ark sent back, the priests returned to the city as watchmen, and the weeping ascent of Olivet

schools.summary: Gill calls the reason for sending the ark back not easy to account for, since the thing would fall into the conspirators’ hands, and settles on the king’s trusting that a sacred object would not be violated and was safest at home; he refuses outright the suggestion of Procopius of Gaza that David could not bear to carry about him a law which accused him of adultery and murder. He takes the word addressed to the priest in its plainer sense of a discerning man, identifies the mount from its olive trees, a mile east of the city, and observes that the antitype of David was often there in his own humiliation.

Ellicott gives the sharpest reason for sending the ark back: recognising that he suffers under Nathan’s sentence, the king will not take it lest he seem to compel the divine presence and blessing. He finds the language describing the priests’ conduct obscure and reconstructs it, with the one priest and the Levites bringing the ark out and setting it down while the crowd gathered, and the other leading that crowd up the mount, the king addressing the first exclusively and merely mentioning the second — which tells us nothing of their standing but much about a day of confusion. On the address he allows either rendering, the change being one vowel, and explains the title by the office the man was now to fill in guiding the king’s course and reporting what events showed of God’s will; he adds that neither Nathan nor Gad appears in this narrative, though both were certainly still living. On the place of waiting he notes that the margin’s plain of the wilderness is followed by the ancient versions, but prefers the text’s the fords, both as a definite place where messengers could find the king and as a position leaving a retreat across the Jordan open. Keil and Delitzsch say simply of the ark that he put his fate into the Lord’s hand; they deny that the interrogative can stand in the address, since the question would concern what the man could not have denied, and repoint the word as a vocative, as Jerome and Luther had done — thou seer, seer being equivalent to prophet, applied to a high priest who received divine answers by the Urim, so that his proper place was the city. On the covered head they see only grief and mourning.

Clarke reads confidence and humility together in the sending back of the ark: it was too precious to expose to his wanderings, and he would not carry out of the city of God the one thing without which public worship could not go on, feeling more for that worship than for his own safety. He explains the priests’ coming out at all — they knew the kingdom had been given to David and had no evidence that he was deposed, so they chose to accompany him with their charge — and gives another ground for sending one of them back, that he was the one organ of public worship and had nothing to fear personally, for the nation had abandoned their king but not their God. On the covered head he notes that it was the attitude of a condemned man as well: the heads of culprits were covered when sentence had passed, as with Haman, and a Roman historian records the same order given over Philota. Wesley adds a care for the priests, whom carrying the ark would have exposed to the rebel’s rage; he has the high priest go up from the ark toward the city, which lay higher, to use his authority in persuading the people to their duty and to wait until all who would be persuaded had come out; and he takes the disputed word in its plainer sense of a discerning man, which suits the king’s purpose, needing prudence and secrecy.

debates.question: Why did David send the ark back into the city?

positions.view: Trusting that a sacred object would not be violated, and was safest at home
It was too precious to expose to his wanderings, and public worship could not go on without it
Out of care for the priests, whom carrying it would have exposed to the rebel’s rage
Lest, suffering under Nathan’s sentence, he seem to compel the divine presence and blessing
He simply put his fate into the Lord’s hand

debates.question: Is the word addressed to Zadok a question or a title?

positions.view: The interrogative cannot stand; repoint it as the vocative thou seer, with Jerome and Luther
Either rendering will do, the change being one vowel; the title fits the office he was now to fill
Take it in its plainer sense, of a discerning man

debates.question: What does the king’s covered head signify?

positions.view: Grief and mourning only
Also the attitude of a condemned man, culprits’ heads being covered once sentence had passed

outliers.claim: Alone in reporting, and refusing, the suggestion of Procopius of Gaza that David could not bear to carry about him a law that accused him of adultery and murder.
Alone in reading the covered head as the mark of a condemned man, citing Haman and a Roman order given over Philota.
Alone in noting that neither Nathan nor Gad appears anywhere in this narrative, though both were certainly still living.

themes: the ark carried out and set down
if I shall find favour in the eyes of the Lord
the fords of the wilderness
a covered head and bare feet
weeping up the ascent of Olivet

31.pericope_label: The prayer that Ahithophel’s counsel be turned to foolishness, and Hushai sent back to defeat it

schools.summary: Henry reckons one good head in such a design worth a thousand good hands: the son was himself no politician, but had got entirely into his interest one who was, and who was the more dangerous for having been all along acquainted with the king’s counsels and affairs, so that to baffle him is to cut off the head of the conspiracy. He marks what the prayer does and does not ask — not against the person but against the counsel, that a wise man might for once advise foolishly, or advising wisely be rejected as foolish, or being followed be defeated of his end — and adds that the king now had more need of soldiers than of counsellors. He will not have the dissimulation justified as a stratagem of war at all, and allows only that a son in arms against his father must stand on his guard against all mankind, and that if he will be deceived let him be deceived. His closing remark is on how soon royal cities change their masters.

Gill has the two priests assisting to frame schemes directly opposite to Ahithophel’s, and placed where they could pass on the secrets of the new court; he reads Hushai’s going back as obedience to the king’s direction and persuasion, in order to serve him to the uttermost.

Ellicott renders the clause about the summit as where men worship, the original indicating a customary act, and takes the place for one of those high places which abounded in Israel; he puts Hushai’s home on the border between Ephraim and Benjamin, supposes him to have been there when the rebellion broke out, and calls his coming the beginning of the answer to the king’s prayer. He also notes that the preposition has dropped out of the Hebrew of the opening clause, leaving it to read literally and David told. On the counsel itself he says plainly that David here counsels fraud and treachery and that Hushai willingly accepts the part assigned him, the narrative stating the facts without justifying them. Keil and Delitzsch read a sanctuary on the summit of the Mount of Olives, probably a bamah of the kind that continued to exist in different places throughout the land even after the building of the temple; they take the title the narrative gives Hushai, the king’s friend, for the office of a privy councillor, and the rent clothes and earth upon the head for the deepest mourning. Of the closing verse they note that the construction marks the two arrivals as contemporaneous, Hushai entering the city as Absalom came to Jerusalem.

Clarke agrees that Ahithophel was well versed in state affairs and that God alone could confound his devices; on the halt for worship he draws the practical lesson that the king stops to pray though in danger of his life, and that prayer and provender never hinder any man’s journey. He explains why Hushai was sent back rather than kept: he was not a warrior but a wise, prudent and discreet man who could serve by gaining intelligence, and he was to form a strict confederacy with the two priests and use their sons as couriers between the city and the king’s place of retreat. His closing reflection is on the vicissitude of human affairs — the greatest king that ever lived, politician, general, poet and prophet, driven from his dominions by his own son and forsaken by his fickle people, proof that none is so exalted that God cannot abase, and none so abased that God cannot exalt. Wesley is shorter on the counsel: the crafty advice must be reckoned among David’s sins, and nevertheless God was pleased to direct this evil advice to a good end; he locates the priests’ sons not in Jerusalem but in a place near it, to which word could easily be sent.

debates.question: How far can the counsel David gives Hushai be defended?

positions.view: It is fraud and treachery and cannot be too strongly condemned, with two things remembered: like frauds have been practised in all ages, and David and Hushai had but slender knowledge of the revelation that enables us to condemn them
It must be reckoned among David’s sins, and nevertheless God directed the evil advice to a good end
It cannot be justified as a stratagem of war at all; the best that can be made of it is that a son in arms must stand on his guard against all mankind

debates.question: What was the place of worship on the summit of the mount?

positions.view: A sanctuary, probably a bamah of the kind that survived the building of the temple
One of the high places that abounded in Israel; the original indicates a customary act, where men worship

outliers.claim: Alone in closing the chapter with a reflection on the vicissitude of human affairs, that none is so exalted that God cannot abase nor so abased that God cannot exalt.
Alone in noting that the construction of the last verse marks the two arrivals as contemporaneous.

themes: turn his counsel into foolishness
a bamah on the summit of Olivet
the king’s friend with rent coat and earth
counsel that cannot be justified
couriers between the city and the retreat
